title: Solo dev, 1,000+ hours, AI art and AI-assisted code: what AI did for my game and what it couldn't
author: SushiMasterPro
selftext:
Hey r/aigamedev, solo dev here 👋



I've been building a browser idle RPG since February, probably 1,000+ hours so far. I've worked in games for 15+ years, but I'm not an artist, and I'm one person.



So I leaned on AI hard, for both sides:

🎨 About 1,000 AI-generated images: 722 items, 77 monsters, 87 UI icons, plus spells, pets, dungeons, events and region maps.

💻 The code is mainly AI-assisted too, using an AI coding assistant for almost everything from features to deploy scripts.



Here's an honest breakdown of where it delivered and where it didn't.



✅ WHAT AI DID FOR THE ART

It took the game from all emoji to something that looks like a real game. As a solo dev I could never have paid for 1,000 icons.

But only once I stopped prompting and built a pipeline:

🔁 Every icon is generated from the game data. A script reads the item list, builds a prompt from the name and description plus a style guide, and saves a small webp.

💾 A manifest stores a hash of each prompt, so only new or changed content gets generated. 20 new items cost 20 images, not 1,000.

💸 Low quality at 1024px downscaled to 128px looks basically the same as high quality at icon size. Around a cent per icon.

🧯 A missing icon falls back to an emoji, so nothing ever breaks.



❌ WHERE THE ART NEEDED ME

👉 One style prompt for everything failed. Half my skill icons were unreadable at 32px on a dark brown panel: brown subjects vanished, and thin things like bows and fishing rods became a one-pixel smudge. I had to write a separate UI style that asks for chunky shapes, no thin lines and strong contrast against that exact background.

👉 Never put the game's name in an image prompt. The model paints it as a title, even when you say "no text".

👉 You can't prompt your way out of a bad crop. I cropped banners to 5:2 and lost the top and bottom of every subject. The fix was generating at the display ratio, not better prompts.

👉 Editing an item's description changed its prompt hash, and the pipeline wanted to replace dozens of good shipped icons with new random ones. AI will happily regenerate things you already liked.



✅ WHAT AI DID FOR THE CODE

Honestly, a lot. Features that would have taken me a week take a day. Tests, tools, analytics, deploy scripts, admin pages, a wiki generated from the game data.

It also makes a solo project feel like a small team, because I can hand it the boring 80% and spend my time on decisions.

I even set it up so it can't finish a task that adds new content until the art for that content exists.



❌ WHERE THE CODE NEEDED ME

👉 Save and sync bugs. Offline progress, two devices, a tab left open for days. AI writes a confident fix for the symptom very fast. Finding the real cause still took me reading logs and player saves.

👉 It doesn't know what it doesn't know. It will work in an old copy of the project without noticing, and an old copy once got deployed over the live game. Now every release checks what's live before anything goes out.

👉 Every "done" needs checking. Tests passing is not the same as the feature working in the browser.



🤔 WHAT AI COULDN'T DO AT ALL



Design.

The progression, balance, quests and numbers are where most of my 1,000 hours went. AI can build any system I describe, but it can't tell me if the system is fun, if a skill feels too slow at level 70, or why players quit on day two.

That part is still the whole job.

If anyone wants to see how it all turned out, the game is free in the browser, no signup needed:

[https://dragonscapeidle.com/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=launch&utm\_content=aigamedev](https://dragonscapeidle.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=launch&utm_content=aigamedev)



I'd love to hear from others shipping real games with AI:

• How do you keep a consistent art style across hundreds of assets?

• Has anyone found a way to make thin objects (bows, staffs, rods) readable at small sizes?

• Where has AI-assisted code burned you the worst?

• Has AI helped you with game design at all, or only with building?  


Happy to answer questions about the pipeline or the workflow 🙏

comments.author: AshenThroneDev
comments.body:
The prompt-hash manifest is the part most people skip and then regret. Two things that bit us doing the same at scale on Ashen Throne, which also ships to phones:

1. File size lies about memory. A 2 MB image can decode to well over 100 MB on a phone, so once you have hundreds of generated assets, budget them by width x height x 4, not kilobytes. A half-res variant for mobile goes a long way.
2. Put the style guide version into the hash. Otherwise the day you tweak the style prompt, half the catalog is the old look and nothing tells you which half.

Curious what didn't work on the code side. That's usually where the honest answers are.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
Both great points, thank you!

The memory one I got lucky on: I generate at 1024 and downscale icons to 128px, so each one is only about 65 KB decoded. But my region maps are 1024x1536, which is around 6 MB each in memory, so I'm going to check those on low-end phones now 👀

The style version one is a real gap for me. I do have a style version number in the hash, but I also added a "rebaseline" command so editing an item's description doesn't regenerate good art. Your comment made me realise: if I tweak the style prompt and then rebaseline, the whole catalog quietly adopts the new hash with the old look, and from then on new items come out in the new style. Exactly the "which half" problem. Going to store the style version per entry so that can't happen silently.

On the code side, the honest answers are almost all about saves (I spend weeks the offline progress and I had to add lot of tracking to find things):

💾 Offline progress. When you come back, the game shows you what happened while you were away, then banks it. The first version re-rolled the random drops when banking, so what you were shown and what you got didn't match. The fix wasn't a patch, it was a rule: apply exactly what was previewed, never simulate twice.

📱 Two devices. An older device saving over newer progress from another device. What actually worked was merging per skill, so XP can never go backwards, and treating quest progress the same way.

🕰️ Old builds. A player with a tab open on an old version came back after 10 hours, and that build didn't know about a new quest chain, so none of the offline time counted toward it. Now the game checks for a newer build before it banks anything, and reloads first if there is one.

💸 Cost. Saving every few seconds per open tab looked fine in testing and burned through the free database quota with about 20 real players.

The pattern in all of them: AI is very fast at a confident fix for the symptom, and very bad at noticing that the bug is really a design rule nobody wrote down. Once the rule is written down, it's great at enforcing it everywhere.

One other disclaimer. This is side project I have full time job that takes lot of time. Sometimes I want to ship too fast something and don't spend enough time to review the AI.

replies.author: AshenThroneDev
replies.body:
That last line is the whole thing. What's worked for us is taking it one step further: every time a bug turns out to be an unwritten rule, the rule becomes a tiny script that fails the build if anything breaks it. "Apply exactly what was previewed" becomes a test that replays a preview and diffs it against the real result, and then the AI can't quietly reintroduce the bug in a file it has never seen.

The two-device one bit us too. Forward-only merging is the right call, but watch anything that can legitimately go down, like a currency balance after a purchase. A max-merge will quietly refund it.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
Yes, that's exactly where I ended up too. A few of the rules are already tests: adding a new save merge without declaring its policy fails the test suite, and a gear doc that's out of date with the game data fails it too. The preview-vs-banked replay test is a great idea, adding that one.

And good call on currency. I learned that one early: only things that can never go down get max-merged (XP, kill counts, quest progress). Gold and inventory are never max-merged, the active device's save wins for those, otherwise a purchase on one device gets quietly refunded by the other, exactly like you said.

Also, a real thank you, because your first comment turned straight into an update that's already live 🙏

📱 Memory: I measured in pixels like you said. 27 big images (8 region maps, 19 news banners) were about 96 MB decoded in total. Phones now get their own versions: maps at 720px wide, banners at 640px. Same images, about 42 MB total, so 57% less.

In practice only one map and one banner are on screen at a time, so what a phone actually holds dropped from about 8.7 MB to 4 MB. The largest map went from 6.0 MB to 3.0 MB, a banner from 2.7 MB to 1.0 MB.

🎨 Style drift: every icon (about 980 of them) now stores a style hash and a content hash separately. Edit a description and it's flagged as a content change, safe to keep. Change the style prompt and those icons are flagged as old style, and my "mark as up to date" command refuses to touch them unless I explicitly force it. The "which half is the old look" problem can't happen silently anymore.

Neither of those would have happened without your comment. Thanks for taking the time!

comments.author: HEXAPONG
comments.body: How do you keep the AI from creating mistakes when changing another feature? For example I’ll had Astra Medium make a night version of my side scroller and in the process it added new character animations that didn’t exist before. Specifically the character randomly was holding a sword when I never prompted it nor is there even a sword in the game. I constantly deal with mistakes like this.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
gpt-image-1 through the API, driven by a script instead of a chat window. That's honestly most of the consistency answer: every image gets the exact same style text, word for word, so nothing drifts between sessions.

What helped the most:

🎨 One fixed style block per category, appended to every prompt. For items it's roughly: "A single video-game inventory icon, centered, on a fully transparent background. Clean semi-realistic painterly RPG style, soft rim lighting, subtle drop shadow. Bold silhouette readable at small sizes, rich saturated colors, no text, no border, no frame." Monsters, places, spells and UI icons each have their own version.

🎯 One subject per image, transparent background, no scene. The less the model has to invent, the more alike everything looks.

📝 The item-specific part is just the name plus its in-game description. The exception is item families: every metal tier of a sword or helmet gets a generated prompt that says "same shape, only the metal colour changes". Before that, Bronze, Iron and Steel Sword came back as three unrelated weapons that just shared a colour, and I had to regenerate 248 tier and plating icons in one go.



📐 Generate big, display small. Downscaling to 128px hides most of the small differences between images.

🔁 Never regenerate something that already looks right. Consistency breaks the moment you "refresh" old art with a new random roll.



And honestly, it's not one-shot. From my git history: about 1,030 images generated, and 375 of them (roughly a third) had to be regenerated at least once, about 500 regenerations in total. That's only what got committed, so the real number of re-rolls is higher.

🧤 The best example is gloves. Runite Gloves is on its 5th version. The last three, all in one day:

1. After locking the shape across metal tiers, every tier came out as a mitten with four fingers and no thumb. The pose was "backs of the hands facing the viewer, fingers up", which hides the thumb, so the model just dropped it.

2. I added "five fingers, thumb clearly separate". Worse: some pairs got five fingers PLUS a thumb, some still had no thumb, and one pair was fused together at the wrists.

3. What finally worked was changing the pose, not the count: four fingers closed together as one group, the thumb as the only separate digit, no splayed fingers, and the two gloves clearly apart. All 22 glove icons got regenerated in each of those last two rounds.

Lesson: if the model keeps miscounting something, don't ask for the right number. Pick a pose where there's nothing to count.

It's not perfect up close, but side by side in an inventory grid it reads as one art style.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
That one is so familiar 😅 What reduced it for me:

🔒 Say what must NOT change, not just what to do. "Make a night version. Do not change characters, animations, items or layout. If you think something else needs changing, ask first." Create rules around it in .md documents. 

📦 Keep each task small, and commit before every task. Then read the diff. If the change touched files that have nothing to do with the task, that's your sword, and you can throw it away in one click. I have also skill that do manual QA just to test things and make me screenshots to spot issues

🌙 For something like a night version, don't let an image model redraw the scene at all. Image models reinterpret the whole picture every time, so a random sword is almost guaranteed eventually. A color tint, darker overlay or palette swap done in code keeps every pixel of the original and can't invent anything.

✅ Turn the rules into checks. If the character must only ever use known animations, a tiny test that fails on unknown ones catches it before you do.

The general pattern: the AI doesn't know what it's not allowed to touch unless you tell it or a test tells it.

comments.author: Worried_Number5115
comments.body:
Nice work! Im building an AI developed app and have the same approach as you. 

I think there’s a ton to be said about using AI to develop and taking the mindset of creative director/ game director & using the code as an engineer, asset pipeline, second opinion, database, etc. 

I like your app design and how it flows so far. You might not want to hear this but I think this game is better suited as an iPhone app. 

I use VSC to organize my file base. If you’re not using it already, it will unlock context for any prompt as the agent will read the relevant files before touching code. This will solve your consistency problem & working on an old copy won’t be possible. 

For me, I would say it burns me the worst with specific visual polish tasks. I’ve gotten it to be able to take screenshots to help identify the grid and do specific tasks but it’s still a bit off. For ex., placed trees are good but not nearly the aesthetic and polish I want. I decided to scope a full “handcrafted” phase where my agent will create an artifact with each map, all current placements, all items, and I’ll be able to modify, remove, or add anything on screen. AI most lacks in this type of visual polishing, which is a major part of any game. I plan to spend a few weeks in this phase. 

It does everything else so well, in my opinion.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
Thanks! And yes, "creative director with a very fast engineering team" is exactly how it feels on good days.

On mobile, you're not wrong. It already runs in the phone browser and a lot of players use it that way, and proper store versions are on the plan once the game is out of beta.

The old copy problem wasn't actually missing context, it was me: I had several copies of the project folder for different features, and one of them was months behind. The fix that stuck was making every release check what's live first, before anything goes out.

Totally agree on visual polish. The handcrafted pass is a great idea, AI gets you 80% of the layout and then the last 20% is where the game actually starts to feel like yours. Good luck with it!

replies.author: heartbroken_nerd
replies.body: What were your image prompts for enemy faceplates / enemy icons / enemy portraits (whatever it is you call yours)? I am curious about everything: the prompt, the style that was consistent across prompts, any issues you had generating many of them in similar artstyle etc.

replies.author: SushiMasterPro
replies.body:
Happy to share, it's all one script so the prompts are exact 🙂



Every enemy prompt is two parts glued together.

🎨 The style part, identical for all 78 enemies:

"A single video-game creature icon, a centered bust/portrait, on a fully transparent background. Clean semi-realistic painterly RPG style, soft rim lighting, bold readable silhouette, rich saturated colors, no text, no border, no frame. Just the creature floating in empty space."

🐲 The content part, built from the game data:

"It depicts a fantasy RPG enemy named "Black Dragon": The oldest thing in the valley. It does not hoard gold, it hoards the bones of everyone who came for its hide."

So the name plus the same flavour text the player reads in the game. If an enemy has no description, it's just the name

Settings: gpt-image-1, quality low, 1024x1024, transparent background, then downscaled to 128px webp. Around a cent each.



What made them consistent:

👉 "Bust/portrait" is doing most of the work. Every enemy gets the same framing, head and shoulders, same scale in the frame, so a chicken and a dragon sit side by side in a list without looking like they came from different games. Full-body enemies would vary a lot more in pose and size.

👉 Transparent background, no scene. The UI draws the panel behind them, so there's nothing for the model to make inconsistent.

👉 The exact same style text every time, from code, never retyped.

Honestly, enemies were the easiest group. Items needed about a third regenerated, but none of the enemy portraits have been redone so far.

Issues I can see in them though:

⚠️ Dark creatures on a dark UI. My panels are dark brown, and the Black Dragon is basically a black shape on brown. I fixed exactly this for UI icons with a separate style ("bright rim light, value clearly lighter than the background"), but I haven't applied it to enemies yet.

⚠️ The model only knows what the prompt says. My goblins are archers in the game, but there's no bow in the goblin portrait, because the prompt is just "Goblin". If a gameplay detail matters visually, it has to be in the description.

comments.author: CrowdGoesWildWoooo
comments.body:
Maybe you can use Astra, if you really don’t want people throwing your work just because it’s AI, the least you can do is make the white balance of your game to be less “warm”. 

I swear AI loves this aesthetic and people would immediately know it’s an AI game and call it slop when they saw that
